extraction.name: MathVista
extraction.description: MATHVISTA is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in visual contexts. It consists of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA), covering diverse mathematical reasoning types, tasks, and visual contexts.
extraction.creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
extraction.citeAs: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao. MATHVISTA: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts. Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: MATHVISTA incorporates 28 existing multimodal datasets, including 9 math-targeted question answering datasets and 19 VQA datasets, and adds 3 newly created datasets: IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA. For MathQA datasets, the authors collected nine multimodal datasets and limited each source dataset to up to 400 examples for balanced representation, yielding 2,666 examples. For VQA datasets, they reviewed more than 70 datasets and collected 19 publicly available datasets containing math-related instances. They designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning, then engaged three expert annotators to manually label 4,949 filtered examples to determine whether they involved mathematical reasoning, using majority voting and limiting each source dataset to 400 examples, resulting in 2,739 examples. For the three new datasets, IQTest examples were sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms, FunctionQA contains 400 examples on functional plots, and PaperQA contains 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface. To ensure data quality, all questions in the new datasets were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and refined through a rigorous review process. Each new dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion among the entire review team.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples having annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data come from 31 source datasets: 19 existing VQA datasets, 9 existing MathQA datasets, and 3 newly annotated datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA). IQTest was sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms. PaperQA used informative academic illustrations including tables, figures, and charts from online education resources, with 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: PaperQA examples were sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation. For VQA datasets, heuristic rules automatically selected examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning by choosing examples with numeric answers or quantity words in the questions. Majority voting was used to finalize labels for whether examples involved mathematical reasoning. For release, the dataset was split into testmini (1,000 examples) and test (5,141 examples). To construct testmini, the authors first randomly sampled questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset, then randomly sampled the remaining questions for each source dataset based on its proportion in the entire set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, the authors reviewed more than 70 datasets and collected 19 publicly available ones containing math-related instances. They designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates: examples with numeric answers or containing quantity words in the questions were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, after which expert annotators manually labeled them to determine whether they involved mathematical reasoning. The authors also conducted several quality checks to address unidentified errors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Examples were annotated with metadata including question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, visual context, and required reasoning skills. For VQA filtering, three expert annotators manually labeled automatically filtered examples to determine whether they involved mathematical reasoning, following detailed instructions and using labels Yes, No, or Unsure. For the three new datasets, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and then refined through a rigorous review process. Each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion among the entire review team. For mathematical reasoning categories, coarse labels could be automatically obtained from source dataset details, and expert annotators manually labeled 1,000 examples from seven candidate reasoning categories to verify automatic annotation quality.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: The authors developed an annotation tool with a GUI for labeling whether a problem involves mathematical reasoning, annotating the three new datasets, and labeling mathematical reasoning skills.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For the newly collected 736 questions, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in an inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%; only 6 questions exhibited disagreements in annotated answers, and these were resolved through discussion among the entire review team. For labeling whether problems involved mathematical reasoning, the authors computed a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775 among three annotators, indicating substantial agreement. To verify automatic annotation of mathematical reasoning categories, expert annotators manually labeled 1,000 examples; 94.1% of examples from automatic and human annotations had the exact same set of reasoning types, and 98.79% of individual labels were identical.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Graduate students in STEM fields; three expert annotators; human annotators for baseline evaluation were required to have a high school diploma or higher.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: EasyOCR; GPT-4; heuristic rules for automatic selection; automatic annotation from source dataset details
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The answer labels for the test set will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination, and the authors will maintain an online evaluation platform. The benchmark is described as part of an ongoing research process, and the authors state they are committed to maintaining the datasets, such as refining potential data noise in response to community feedback, and to evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Language; grade level; educational attainment for human annotators
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to facilitate the development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios and evaluate research progress of LLMs and LMMs. The paper states that AI agents with strong mathematical reasoning capabilities in visual contexts have real-world applications in educational disciplines, logical queries about statistical data, theorem proving, and scientific discovery. It also states that MATHVISTA will play a critical role in the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that source datasets were limited to 400 examples each to ensure balanced representation. It also reports that larger numbers of few-shot examples can introduce bias in demonstrations for some models. In the benchmark limitations, the authors state there may be gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals, and that annotations were sourced from original data providers, leading to heterogeneous annotation formats and structures.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark has several acknowledged limitations. There may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Its focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts in specific domains like science and college-level math makes high-quality data collection more labor-intensive than for textual-only or general-purpose datasets, raising concerns about scalability and generalizability to other domains. Only 85.6% of examples have annotations, and because annotations were sourced from original data providers, they lack a unified format and structure. The study focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent foundation models. The authors also note that future iterations should encompass a broader array of problems and visual contexts and provide unified and comprehensive annotations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning capabilities of foundation models in visual contexts. It is intended for model development validation and standard evaluation. MATHVISTA is divided into two subsets: testmini, containing 1,000 examples intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources, and test, containing 5,141 examples for standard evaluation. The benchmark is used for deterministic evaluation with accuracy scores.
